pageCache.pageTitle: Newton Blossomville CE School - Wraparound Care
pageCache.text:
Wraparound Care
Morning Breakfast Club
The breakfast club runs in school from 8.15am to 8.45am at a cost of £3.50 per session.
A cereal breakfast is provided along with a drink. Children have activities available to them such as; construction, art activities and some fresh air before school starts.
Please contact the school office to book a place.
After School Care - Tea Time Club
We are pleased to offer daily after school care in conjunction with Tickford Park Primary School (TPPS) in Newport Pagnell.
The Tickford Park Primary School Tea Time Club is available to children at Newton Blossomville CE First School until 6.00pm each day in term time. The club offers after school care with some activities and a light meal.
Children are collected by minibus with an additional member of TPPS staff - collecting children from Newton Blossomville CE School at 3.30pm, and then collecting from North Crawley CE School, arriving at TPPS at approximately 4.05pm.
Pick up time from TPPS is no later than 6.00pm.
There are limited places available. The transport is free of charge and each session costs £14.50.
Bookings should be made directly with TPPS by contacting them on 01908 610431 who will organise the relevant registration and booking forms to be sent to you. One week's notice is required before your child can start attending the Tea Time Club.
Please also email the school office (office@newtonblossomvilleschool.co.uk) to confirm which days your child will be attending the club.

pageCache.pageTitle: Newton Blossomville CE School - Religious Education
pageCache.text:
Religious Education
At our Voluntary Controlled (VC) First Schools, Religious Education (RE) is a core part of our vibrant curriculum. We introduce children to the fascinating world of religion and worldviews, laying the foundation for a lifelong journey of curiosity and respect.
We carefully align to the locally agreed syllabus set by our Local Authority and use elements of the Oxford Diocesan curriculum. This ensures our teaching is balanced, inclusive, and tailored to our community context in an age-appropriate way.
Our Approach to RE We believe that high-quality RE is essential for helping children understand the complex world around them. Our inquiry-based curriculum is designed around three main pillars:
Exploring Religions and worldviews: Discovering the stories, traditions, festivals, and practices of different faiths and non-religious worldviews, preparing children for life in a multi-secular Britain.
Enquiring into Big Questions: Engaging with significant questions about meaning, purpose, and values to develop personal empathy, kindness, and respect.
Celebrating Diversity: Fostering an inclusive environment where every child’s unique background, culture, and beliefs are valued, shared, and celebrated.
What We Study In line with our local syllabus and our Church of England heritage, Christianity forms the core of our RE curriculum. Alongside this, the focus is Judaism, which our children explore in depth.
Our pupils learn about other major world faiths and non-religious worldviews represented in modern Britain and our local Milton Keynes community.
Because we are a First School, we bring RE to life using hands-on, creative approaches suitable for young minds:
Storytelling: Using sacred texts, parables, and modern stories to explore faith and morality.
Artefacts & Symbols: Giving children tangible objects, clothing, and symbols to explore and discuss.
Vibrant Festivals: Exploring celebrations like Harvest, Sukkot, Diwali, Christmas, and Eid through art, music, and food.
Reflective Discussion: Encouraging children to ask "big questions" and express their own thoughts safely.
Why RE Matters in the Early Years
RE is not about persuading children to believe a certain faith. Instead, it is about giving them the tools to become thoughtful, open-minded, and compassionate citizens. It helps our youngest children build a strong sense of identity while developing deep respect for the diverse world they are growing up in.

Local SEND Offer
Milton Keynes Local Authority SEND Offer
The Children and Families Bill 2014 requires local authorities and schools to publish and regularly update information about services for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) aged 0-25. This is known as the 'Local Offer'. It aims to provide clear information to families about available support and resources, enabling informed decision-making and fostering an inclusive educational environment.
Read the Milton Keynes City Council Local Authority SEND Offer here
Visit the Milton Keynes City Council Local Authority SEND offer Facebook page here

SEND
Special Educational Need and Disability
At Newton Blossomville CE School, provision for pupils with SEND is co-ordinated by the Village Schools Federation SENDCo Mrs Adey Underwood (Inclusion Lead).
Contact: senco@villageschoolsfederation.co.uk
At Newton Blossomville CE School, we believe that every pupil deserves the support they need to thrive. Our SEND provision is designed to ensure that all pupils, regardless of their needs, feel included, valued, and able to reach their full potential. Our aim is to make sure that every pupil gets the right support, at the right time. We know that parents and carers are key partners in their child’s education and that is why we are here to listen to your concerns, answer your questions, and work with you every step of the way. At Newton Blossomville CE School, inclusion is at the heart of what we do and we strive to create a school where all pupils can feel safe, make friends, and enjoy learning—no matter their starting point or the challenges they face. Together, we can help every pupil shine.
As an inclusive school, we offer a range of provisions tailored to support children with various Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), including those with social, communication, and interaction needs, learning difficulties, emotional and mental health needs, and physical needs.
We endeavour to promptly identify each child’s particular needs and respond appropriately, enabling them to make progress alongside their peers. Newton Blossomville CE School is committed to providing an inclusive, quality education to all pupils across our family of schools, promoting equality of access and opportunity in all areas of the curriculum. Our children learn in happy, exciting, respectful, and supportive environments, equipping them with the knowledge and cultural capital necessary for success in life.
There is a shared expectation that all pupils, regardless of their specific needs, should receive inclusive teaching that facilitates optimal progress and fosters a sense of belonging within the wider school community. The Village Federation Schools (VSF) implements a systematic approach to ensure continuity of provision, aligned with the Government’s SEND Code of Practice (2014) and our SEN Policy. Furthermore, the Local Authority’s local offer effectively communicates the services available to parents and young people, ensuring clarity in our provision for SEND.
Our SEND policy can be found here

pageCache.text:
Inclusion
Special Educational Need and Disability
Newton Blossomville CE School strives to provide an inclusive, quality education to all pupils across our family of schools, whilst promoting equality of access and opportunity to all areas of the curriculum. Our children learn in happy, exciting, respectful and supportive environments, providing them with the knowledge and cultural capital needed to succeed in life. We are committed to meeting the needs of all pupils, including those with special educational needs, encouraging all children to fulfil their full potential, whilst embracing children’s individual talents and needs. There is a shared expectation that all pupils, regardless of their specific needs, should be offered inclusive teaching which will enable them to make the best possible progress in school and feel that they are a valued member of the wider school community.
There are some children who may require additional support during their school life and the VFS offers a range of additional provision to support children across all areas of need. Children may join us with SEND already identified and others may be identified as potentially needing support.
A systematic approach is essential within our village schools, with processes in place to ensure continuity of provision. The Government’s SEND Code of Practice (2014), provides the framework for these processes and the VSF’s SEN Policy is written to reflect Government policy in the Code of Practice and clearly outlines the processes in place.
Additionally, the Local Authority’s local offer is to enable parents and young people to see more clearly what services are available, communicating their provision for SEND.
Provision for pupils with SEND is co-ordinated by the school SENDCo , Mrs Adey Underwood.
CONTACT: senco@villageschoolsfederation.co.uk

pageCache.text:
EYFS Curriculum
Village Schools Federation EYFS Skills Progression
Our EYFS Skills Progression document supports high-quality teaching and learning throughout the Early Years Foundation Stage. It is designed to ensure that children develop the essential knowledge, skills and behaviours needed for future success through carefully planned, progressive learning experiences.
The document identifies the key skills children will work towards across all areas of learning, including communication and language, personal, social and emotional development, physical development, literacy, mathematics and understanding the world. Skills are carefully sequenced so that learning builds progressively over time, allowing children to develop confidence, independence and deeper understanding.
Teachers use the Skills Progression document to inform their weekly and daily planning, ensuring that activities are purposeful, developmentally appropriate and tailored to meet the needs of individual children. It helps staff identify what children need to learn next and supports consistent expectations across the EYFS.
The document also ensures a balance between adult-directed teaching and child-initiated learning. Through high-quality interactions, play-based experiences and carefully planned environments, children are given opportunities to practise and apply their developing skills in meaningful contexts.
Our EYFS Skills Progression document is firmly rooted in the Early Years Foundation Stage Framework and reflects our commitment to providing a nurturing, ambitious and engaging curriculum that supports every child to thrive.

pageCache.pageTitle: Newton Blossomville CE School - KS1 Curriculum
pageCache.text:
KS1 Curriculum
Village Schools Federation Long Term Curriculum Overview
Our Key Stage 1 long-term curriculum overview is organised through a carefully structured two-year cycle, designed to provide a broad, balanced, and engaging curriculum for all pupils, including those within mixed-age classes. Built around rich thematic learning, the curriculum enables children to make meaningful connections across subjects while developing knowledge, skills, and understanding progressively over time.
The cyclical structure of Cycle A and Cycle B ensures full curriculum coverage without unnecessary repetition, allowing pupils to experience a diverse range of increasingly challenging learning opportunities as they move through Key Stage 1. Overall, the curriculum reflects a thoughtful and ambitious approach that combines academic achievement with creativity, personal development, and cultural understanding. It is designed to make learning immersive, connected, and relevant, fostering curiosity about themselves, their communities, and the wider world.
The academic year is divided into three overarching thematic strands: People and Communities, Buildings and Places, and The Natural World. Each strand is explored across the autumn, spring, and summer terms through memorable and child-centred topics. In Cycle A, for example, pupils begin by exploring personal identity and community through topics such as This is Me! and Respect Our World. During the spring term, the focus shifts toward history and geography-based learning through themes like My City and Castles. In the summer term, the curriculum broadens children’s understanding of global diversity and environments with topics such as Where is Africa? and Life in Africa.
The curriculum is deliberately cross-curricular.
English is closely linked to each topic, allowing pupils to develop writing and reading skills through purposeful contexts. This approach ensures literacy skills are embedded authentically within the wider curriculum rather than taught in isolation.
Mathematics follows a progressive mastery model, with both Year 1 and Year 2 objectives carefully mapped throughout the year. Key mathematical concepts such as place value, addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, fractions, measurement, geometry, and statistics are revisited and developed incrementally. The structure demonstrates clear progression while ensuring opportunities for consolidation and application.
Science learning is similarly sequenced to build children’s understanding of the natural and physical world. The curriculum promotes enquiry, observation, investigation, and scientific vocabulary development, helping children become increasingly curious and analytical learners.
Foundation subjects are integrated meaningfully into each termly theme. Computing lessons develop digital literacy and programming skills alongside safe and responsible technology use. History and geography are taught through engaging contexts that encourage children to understand chronology, place, culture, and human impact on the environment. Art and Design Technology provide opportunities for creativity, evaluation, problem-solving, and technical skill development through practical projects linked to each topic.
The curriculum also places significant emphasis on pupils’ personal development. PSHER supports emotional wellbeing, relationships, responsibility, and citizenship. RE introduces children to different beliefs, values, and traditions, helping foster respect and understanding of diversity. Music and PE contribute to children’s creative expression, confidence, teamwork, coordination, and physical health.

pageCache.pageTitle: Newton Blossomville CE School - Collective Worship
pageCache.text:
Collective Worship
The Place of Collective Worship in our Church of England Schools
“Whatever we do, we work at it with all our heart” — Colossians 3:23
Across The Village Schools Federation, Collective Worship serves as the heartbeat to the daily rhythm of life in our schools. Guided by our biblical text from Colossians, we aspire to nurture and inspire every child to experience life in all its fullness.
Our schools are rooted in inclusive Christian values that enable everyone to flourish by building knowledge, confidence, and resilience for the future. By coming together daily by invitation, we explore and express our school vision in a unified, inclusive manner. We endeavour for our worship to be transformative—a space where children leave refreshed, re-energised, and inspired to "be the best we can be”.
Where and How We Worship
Collective Worship takes place across diverse settings: within classrooms, on our communal carpet areas (our equivalent to a school hall), throughout our outdoor learning environments, in the local community, and inside our parish churches. Moments of spiritual reflection and deeper questioning are not confined to these slots; they occur organically across the wider life of our schools.
We signpost worship as a distinct, special time by the ringing of bells. Children actively participate by preparing the focus table with meaningful objects that reflect the day's theme. This focus table moves through the liturgical calendar, displaying changing seasonal colours and stoles, while three candles are lit to help us focus on the nature of God.
Worshippers sit together in a variety of formations—often in a mixed-age horseshoe shape. The facilitator deliberately sits at a similar physical level to the children to encourage shared ownership, dignity, and equality.
Our Rich and Varied Pattern of Worship
Our weekly pattern follows the seasons and festivals of the Church year alongside special days of celebration.
Worship reflects aspects of our wider curriculum to foster spiritual growth and introduce children to the impact of faith through a flexible weekly cycle of distinct sessions:
Value Worship: We introduce a core Christian value using resources like Roots and Fruits or Oscar Out of the Box, linking it directly back to our school vision.
Story & Theme Worship: We share stories Jesus told, look at his life, explore values from other religious traditions, or learn about historical figures who served in humility.
Singing Assembly: We sing a range of well-known and seasonal songs, inviting children to choose favourites and pause for brief silent reflections.
Visual Worship & Spirituality: We use nature, still life, imagery, or short video clips to engage the children in deep reflection on creation and charitable concerns.
Celebration Assembly: We celebrate individual gifts, abilities, and skills within our community, recognising each person as a valued ‘child of God’.
A typical daily act of worship follows a four-part journey:
The Gathering greeting setting our intention;
The Word via a Bible reading, story, or message;
The Exploration bringing the theme alive through drama, dance, song, images, or poetry;
The Response & Sending Out offering dedicated time for prayer, reflection, and quiet thoughts so the impact of worship is carried forward into the working day
Leadership and Community Partnerships
We want our pupils to know they are individually valued, encouraged, and affirmed. Therefore, all members of our community are empowered to lead and shape worship, including school staff, clergy, visitors, and the children themselves through active planning, leading, and evaluation.
Members of the local clergy are a deeply valued part of our school community, leading worship regularly. We also enjoy a strong partnership with the Bridgebuilder Trust, who visit throughout the year to enrich our assemblies.
